name: Kagbeni
tagline: A medieval village at the door of Upper Mustang
meta_description: Kagbeni at 2,810 m: the mud-walled village at the Kali Gandaki confluence, its 15th-century Sakya gompa, ancestor rites and the gate to Upper Mustang.
summary: Kagbeni is a compact, mud-walled village at about 2,810 m where the Jhong Khola from Muktinath meets the Kali Gandaki, 11 km north of Jomsom. It has a 15th-century Sakya gompa, a ruined palace, tunnel-like lanes and the checkpoint where the restricted area of Upper Mustang begins. Hindus come here to make offerings for their ancestors.
intro: Kagbeni feels like the first village of Tibet. Its houses are packed tightly together on a terrace above the river, with lanes so narrow that in places they run beneath the houses as dark tunnels. Walls are of mud brick and stone, painted in ochre and white. Above them rises the red bulk of Kag Chode gompa and the crumbling walls of the old khar, or palace. Green fields of barley and buckwheat spread out below on the river terraces.

This is where two valleys meet. The Jhong Khola, which flows down from Muktinath, joins the Kali Gandaki just below the village, and the old trails to Muktinath, to Jomsom and north into Lo all pass through. At the northern edge of Kagbeni a sign and a police checkpost mark the limit of the restricted area of Upper Mustang. Without the special permit, foreigners may go no further up the Kali Gandaki.

We recommend at least one night here. Kagbeni is only 30 minutes by jeep from Jomsom and two to three hours on foot, and it makes the best first stop for anyone heading to Muktinath or Upper Mustang. Wander the lanes in the late afternoon, visit the gompa, walk down to the confluence, and then sleep in one of the old houses converted into lodges. The Red House Lodge is the best known of them.

story.title: A gate on the road between Lo and the south
paras: Kagbeni's position made it important for as long as people have travelled this valley. Every caravan going between Lo and the southern Kali Gandaki, and every pilgrim heading to Muktinath, passed through here. The village name is often explained as 'kag', a blockage or checkpoint, and 'beni', the Nepali word for a river confluence. For centuries it was a fortified village, with its houses packed defensively around the khar and its lanes easy to close off. Walking into it today, you can still see that design.

In the 15th century Kagbeni lay within the sphere of the kingdom of Lo, founded by Ame Pal in the late 14th century. Kag Chode Thupten Samphel Ling, the Sakya gompa that still dominates the village, is traditionally dated to 1429. Its monks once served the whole surrounding area of Baragaun, the 'twelve villages' between Kagbeni and Muktinath. The khar beside it, now partly ruined, housed the local rulers who controlled the crossroads and taxed the trade that passed through.

Today Kagbeni sits in Baragaun Muktikshetra rural municipality, with a population of just over 500 at the 2011 census. Life still runs on barley, buckwheat and apples, now joined by tourism. Since Upper Mustang opened to foreigners in 1992, Kagbeni has been the point where trekkers show their restricted area permits. The jeep road north to Lo Manthang runs past the village, but the lanes inside are still too narrow for anything wider than a horse. Evenings, when the jeeps stop, it is very quiet.

legend: Hindu pilgrims say that offerings made at the confluence of rivers carry special merit, and that the meeting of the Kali Gandaki and the stream from Muktinath at Kagbeni is among the most powerful places in Nepal for shraddha, the rites for dead ancestors. Pilgrims believe that rice balls offered here bring peace to the souls of parents and grandparents, which is why many Hindu families stop at Kagbeni on the way to or from Muktinath.
people: Kagbeni's families are part of the Baragaun communities between Kagbeni and Muktinath. They speak a Tibetan dialect at home and Nepali widely, and many use the surname Gurung or Bista. Most are Buddhist, centred on Kag Chode gompa, and farm barley, buckwheat, apples and vegetables on irrigated terraces. Many households now run lodges or work in trekking and transport, and some move to Pokhara or Kathmandu in winter.

untold.fact: Kagbeni marks the southern limit of the Upper Mustang restricted area. North of the checkpoint at the edge of the village, foreigners need a special restricted area permit on top of the usual ACAP permit and must travel with a licensed guide.

untold.fact: Kagbeni had just 555 residents at the 2011 census, yet it is regarded as one of the oldest villages in the Nepal Himalaya, and it lies between two rivers held sacred by Hindus.

The Jhong Khola, which joins the Kali Gandaki at Kagbeni, flows down from the Muktinath valley at the foot of the Thorong La, so Kagbeni sits where the Annapurna Circuit trail meets the old road to Lo.

taste.name: Sea-buckthorn juice
taste.text: Sea-buckthorn is a thorny shrub of the dry Himalaya whose small orange berries make a sharp, sour juice high in vitamin C. Lodges in Kagbeni serve it hot or cold, and it is sold in bottles around Mustang. Try a glass after the dusty walk from Jomsom.

highlights.title: Kag Chode gompa
highlights.text: The red Sakya monastery above the village, traditionally dated to 1429, with an assembly hall of old statues and wall paintings and a small community of young monks. Its roof gives a view over Kagbeni's flat roofs to the Kali Gandaki and Nilgiri.

highlights.title: The tunnel lanes
highlights.text: Kagbeni's lanes are narrow, twisting and in places roofed over by houses, so you walk through short dark tunnels between courtyards. Prayer wheels, kani gates and old wooden doors line the way. Walk them slowly with a guide in the late afternoon.

highlights.title: The confluence
highlights.text: Below the village, the Jhong Khola meets the Kali Gandaki on a wide gravel plain. Hindu pilgrims perform shraddha for their ancestors here, and some search the riverbed for shaligram fossils. The view upstream into Upper Mustang is the first look at the land of Lo.

highlights.title: The old khar
highlights.text: The ruined palace beside the gompa once housed the local rulers who controlled this crossroads and its trade. Its high mud walls are slowly crumbling, so view from the lanes rather than climbing on them. It is a reminder of how important Kagbeni once was.

highlights.title: The Upper Mustang gate
highlights.text: At the northern edge of the village a checkpost marks the start of the restricted area of Upper Mustang. Trekkers show their permits here. Even without a permit, you can stand at the edge and look north up the Kali Gandaki towards Lo.

highlights.title: Walk to Jharkot and Muktinath
highlights.text: A steady half-day climb east up the Jhong Khola valley to Khingar and Jharkot, with its fort and gompa, and on to Muktinath. The best way to reach the temple, and much better for acclimatisation than going up by jeep.

how_to_reach.text: Kagbeni is ≈ 11 km north of Jomsom, about 30 minutes by jeep on the road to Muktinath and Lo Manthang. Shared jeeps and buses run from Jomsom; we use private jeeps. From Pokhara, allow 8–9 hours by road via Beni and Jomsom.
Fly Pokhara–Jomsom (about 20 minutes, early morning only), then drive 30 minutes or walk up the river. Flights are often delayed by wind or cloud; keep a spare day.
From Jomsom, walk 2.5–3 hours north along the Kali Gandaki riverbed via Ekle Bhatti, with the wind at your back after late morning. From Muktinath, it is 3–4 hours down via Jharkot and Khingar.

where_to_stay: Kagbeni has around fifteen lodges, several in old village houses. The Red House Lodge, in a restored traditional building with its own old prayer room, is the one we use most: rooms are simple but warm, and the setting inside the old village is the point. Other lodges near the checkpost are newer, with attached bathrooms and good views over the confluence. There is no luxury hotel; for that, stay at Shinta Mani Mustang in Jomsom and visit Kagbeni by day, though you then miss the village in the evening light.
tips: Spend the night: the lanes are best in late afternoon and early morning, when day-trippers from Jomsom have gone.
Walk up from Jomsom in the late morning so the afternoon wind pushes you north rather than into your face.
Keep your permits handy; the checkpost at the north end of the village checks ACAP and Upper Mustang papers.
If you plan shraddha at the confluence, bring or arrange the materials and a priest through your guide in advance.
Do not climb the ruined walls of the khar; they are fragile mud brick and part of the village's heritage.

experiences.title: Morning puja at Kag Chode gompa
experiences.summary: Visit Kagbeni's Sakya monastery, traditionally founded in 1429, at the hour of morning prayers. Sit at the back of the assembly hall while young monks chant, then climb to the roof for the view over the village, the confluence and the road north to Lo.
body: Kag Chode Thupten Samphel Ling belongs to the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism, the same school as the main monasteries of Lo Manthang. It is traditionally dated to 1429, when this part of the Kali Gandaki lay within the sphere of the kingdom of Lo. The red-walled gompa stands above the village beside the ruined khar, and its monks once served all the villages of Baragaun. It is the largest and oldest religious building in the village.

We go early, when the monks gather in the assembly hall for morning prayers. Most are young novices from Mustang and nearby areas who study here. You sit quietly at the back while the chanting, drums and horns fill the dim room. Afterwards, the caretaker or a senior monk can show you the old statues, thangkas and wall paintings, some of which are faded with age and smoke from butter lamps.

Before you leave, climb to the roof. From here you look across Kagbeni's packed flat roofs to the gravel plain where the Jhong Khola meets the Kali Gandaki, and north up the valley towards Upper Mustang. Nilgiri rises to the south. A donation is expected; we suggest NPR 300–500 per person. Photography inside the hall is usually not allowed, so ask first. Allow about an hour and a half in all.

faqs.q: How old is the monastery in Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Kag Chode Thupten Samphel Ling is traditionally dated to 1429, in the 15th century, when the area was within the sphere of the kingdom of Lo. It belongs to the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism. Parts of the building have been repaired over the centuries, but it remains the spiritual centre of Kagbeni.

faqs.q: What time are prayers at Kagbeni monastery?
faqs.a: Morning prayers usually begin around sunrise, often 6–7 am, and may last an hour. Times vary with the season and the monastic calendar, and the monks may be away for rituals elsewhere. Your guide or lodge can confirm the evening before. Visitors are welcome to sit quietly at the back.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Kag Chode gompa?
faqs.a: Usually not inside the assembly hall, and never during prayers without permission. Many monasteries in Mustang restrict interior photography to protect old paintings and for religious reasons. Photography on the roof and courtyard is generally fine. Always ask the caretaker first and respect a refusal.

experiences.title: Ancestor rites at the Kagbeni confluence
experiences.summary: For Hindu travellers, a chance to perform shraddha or pinda daan for departed parents and ancestors at the meeting of the Kali Gandaki and the stream from Muktinath, with a priest arranged in advance. Non-Hindu visitors can watch respectfully from a distance.
body: Hindus believe that a confluence of rivers is a place of special merit, and Kagbeni's confluence, on the way to Muktinath, is one of the most important in Nepal for rites for the dead. Shraddha or pinda daan involves offering balls of rice, sesame and other items to the ancestors, with mantras recited by a priest. Many families from India and Nepal make the journey for this alone, often in the autumn fortnight of Pitri Paksha.

We arrange a priest and the materials in advance through contacts in Kagbeni and Jomsom, since few priests live here year-round. The rite is performed on the gravel by the water, usually in the morning. It takes about an hour, depending on how many ancestors are remembered. Wear clean, modest clothes; men are often asked to remove shirts for parts of the ritual, so bring a shawl. Your guide will help translate if needed.

Non-Hindu visitors are welcome to watch from a respectful distance but should not photograph families during the ritual without permission. In autumn and spring the river is low and the gravel bed is easy to walk; in the monsoon the water rises fast and rituals move higher up the bank. Many families then continue to Muktinath the same day by jeep. Allow a quiet hour afterwards before moving on. It is a moving morning.

faqs.q: Why do Hindus perform shraddha at Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Hindus consider river confluences especially sacred for rites for the dead, and Kagbeni lies at the meeting of the Kali Gandaki and the stream from Muktinath, a major Vaishnava pilgrimage site. Offering pinda (rice balls) here is believed to bring peace to departed ancestors. Many pilgrims combine it with a visit to Muktinath.

faqs.q: Can I find a priest in Kagbeni for pinda daan?
faqs.a: Sometimes, especially in the busy pilgrimage seasons, but it is safer to arrange one in advance through your travel company or a contact in Jomsom. The priest will tell you what materials to bring, such as rice, sesame, kusha grass and flowers, or can supply them for an agreed fee. Confirm the day and time before you arrive.

faqs.q: When is the best time for shraddha at Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Shraddha can be performed at any time, but Pitri Paksha, the fortnight for ancestors in September or October, is the most popular. Autumn also has low rivers and clear weather. In the monsoon, from June to August, the river runs high and fast, so rituals take place higher on the bank. Dates follow the lunar calendar.

experiences.title: Kagbeni's tunnel lanes and the old khar
experiences.summary: A slow walk through one of the best-preserved fortified villages in Nepal: narrow lanes that tunnel beneath houses, mud-brick walls, prayer wheels, kani gates, guardian figures at the village edges and the ruined palace that once controlled the crossroads.
body: Kagbeni was built for defence. Houses are packed tightly around the khar and the gompa, sharing walls, and the lanes between them are narrow enough to close off quickly. In places the lanes pass under the houses themselves, so you walk through short dark tunnels lit by a single opening. Upstairs, families live above the animals and storerooms, and use the flat roofs for drying crops and firewood. It is a village made for walking.

Your guide will point out the details. Small prayer wheels sit in wall niches; kani gates painted inside with mandalas mark the entrances; and at the village edges stand old clay guardian figures, local protectors meant to keep harmful spirits out. Water channels run beside the lanes to the fields. Some houses have been turned into lodges, others are empty, and a few are slowly being restored. Look up as well as around.

We finish beside the old khar, the palace of the local rulers, whose high mud walls are now partly in ruins. Do not climb on them; they are fragile. In the late afternoon the low sun turns the ochre walls warm and long shadows fill the lanes, the best light for photographs. Ask before photographing people in doorways or courtyards, especially older residents. Finish with tea on a lodge rooftop.

faqs.q: What is the khar in Kagbeni?
faqs.a: The khar is the old fort-palace beside Kag Chode gompa, once the seat of the local rulers who controlled the crossroads at Kagbeni and taxed trade on the route between Lo and the south. It is now partly ruined. You can see it from the lanes and the gompa roof, but its fragile mud walls should not be climbed.

faqs.q: What are the clay figures at Kagbeni?
faqs.a: At the edges of Kagbeni stand old clay figures that act as protectors of the village, meant to keep harmful spirits and misfortune out. Such guardian figures are found in several old villages of Mustang. Treat them with respect: do not touch them, sit near them or pose for joke photographs with them.

faqs.q: Is Kagbeni good for photography?
faqs.a: Yes, it is one of the best villages in Mustang for photography. The tunnel lanes, ochre walls, Kag Chode gompa and confluence give strong subjects, and the late-afternoon and early-morning light is warm and low. The wind and dust after midday can be harsh on equipment. Always ask before photographing people.

experiences.title: Walk from Kagbeni to Muktinath via Jharkot
experiences.summary: A steady half-day climb of about 900 m from Kagbeni up the Jhong Khola valley to Khingar, Jharkot and Muktinath, through fields, poplars and old fortified villages, with the Dhaulagiri and Nilgiri ranges behind you. The best way to arrive at the temple.
body: From Kagbeni the trail climbs east above the Jhong Khola, the stream that flows down from Muktinath. It is a steady ascent of about 900 m over 10–12 km, mostly on old footpaths that stay away from the jeep road. Behind you, the view opens to Dhaulagiri, Tukuche Peak and Nilgiri, and across the valley you can see the old village of Jhong with its ruined fort on the opposite slope.

Halfway up is Khingar, a small village among poplar trees and fields, and then Jharkot, a fortified village on a spur with a ruined dzong, a gompa and a Tibetan medicine centre. Jharkot is worth a slow hour, and it makes a good lunch stop. Its lanes have the same tunnels and mud walls as Kagbeni, with far fewer visitors. Lodges here serve good dal-bhat and Tibetan bread. Take your time here.

The last hour climbs to Ranipauwa, the village beside Muktinath temple, at about 3,700 m. Walking up gives your body time to adjust; people who drive straight up from Jomsom often feel the altitude more. You can visit the temple in the afternoon or the next morning. Carry water, sun protection and a warm layer; the wind picks up after midday. Luggage can go ahead by jeep from Kagbeni. It is worth the effort.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk from Kagbeni to Muktinath?
faqs.a: Allow 4–5 hours for the walk up, gaining about 900 m over 10–12 km, plus time at Jharkot. Coming down from Muktinath to Kagbeni takes about 3 hours. The trail is a good footpath with no technical sections, but the altitude makes it tiring. Walk slowly and start early to avoid the afternoon wind.

faqs.q: Is it better to walk or drive to Muktinath?
faqs.a: Walking from Kagbeni is better for acclimatisation and far more interesting, passing Khingar and Jharkot. Driving from Jomsom takes about 1–1.5 hours and suits pilgrims short of time, older travellers and those with mobility limits. If you drive, rest on arrival, walk slowly and do not plan anything strenuous the same day.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Jharkot?
faqs.a: Jharkot is a fortified village on a spur below Muktinath, with a ruined dzong, a Sakya gompa, a small centre for traditional Tibetan medicine and tunnel-like lanes similar to Kagbeni's. It sees far fewer visitors than Muktinath. It is the natural lunch stop on the walk up from Kagbeni, with lodges and views down the valley.

faqs.q: Do I need a special permit for Kagbeni?
faqs.a: No restricted area permit is needed for Kagbeni itself. You need an ACAP permit (NPR 3,000; SAARC nationals NPR 1,000) and a TIMS card, and since April 2023 a licensed guide in conservation areas. North of the checkpost at the village edge, Upper Mustang requires a separate restricted area permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Kagbeni from Jomsom?
faqs.a: Kagbeni is about 11 km north of Jomsom: 30 minutes by jeep, or 2.5–3 hours on foot along the Kali Gandaki riverbed. Walk in the late morning so the wind is behind you. Shared jeeps run often from Jomsom; private jeeps can be arranged for a half-day or one-way trip.

faqs.q: Is Kagbeni worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes. Day visitors see the village at its busiest and windiest. An overnight stay lets you walk the lanes in the late-afternoon light, attend morning prayers at Kag Chode gompa and set off early for Muktinath or Upper Mustang. Several lodges are in old village houses, including the Red House Lodge.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Kagbeni sits at about 2,810 m, a little higher than Jomsom. Most people adjust easily after a night in Jomsom or Marpha. It is a good place to spend a night before climbing to Muktinath (≈ 3,710 m) or heading north into Upper Mustang, where villages lie between 3,500 and 3,900 m.

faqs.q: What does Kagbeni mean?
faqs.a: The name is often explained as 'kag', a blockage or checkpoint, and 'beni', the Nepali word for a river confluence. It fits the village well: it sits where the Jhong Khola from Muktinath meets the Kali Gandaki, and it controlled the trail between Lo and the south. Today it is still the checkpoint for Upper Mustang.

faqs.q: Can I visit Upper Mustang from Kagbeni without a permit?
faqs.a: No. North of Kagbeni's checkpost, foreigners need a restricted area permit for Upper Mustang, issued through a registered trekking agency for groups of at least two with a licensed guide. Since a November 2025 government decision the fee is reported as USD 50 per person per day, replacing USD 500 for 10 days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kagbeni?
faqs.a: March to May and September to November are best, with clear skies and days of 12–20 °C. Winter is cold, with nights to −10 °C, but sunny and quiet. Kagbeni is in the rain shadow, so the monsoon brings little rain here, though roads and flights from Pokhara can be disrupted in July and August.

faqs.q: Is Kagbeni suitable for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Kagbeni is small, safe and fascinating for children, with tunnel lanes, a monastery with young monks and a riverbed to search for fossils. The altitude is moderate at 2,810 m. Keep children warm in the evenings, watch them near the river, and keep walking days short. Lodges are simple but welcoming.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Lodges serve Thakali-style dal-bhat, Tibetan dishes such as thukpa and momo, buckwheat bread, apple pie and local sea-buckthorn juice. Food is simple and filling. Try buckwheat dishes and local apples in autumn. Vegetarian food is easy to find, and many lodges cook to order in their family kitchens.
